source.title: Copy Suppression: Comprehensively Understanding a Motif in Language Model Attention Heads
source.authors: Callum McDougall; Arthur Conmy; Cody Rushing; Thomas McGrath; Neel Nanda

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The original study directly tests the proposed role using behavioral analysis, circuit measurements, and ablations. It is not a reproduction of an earlier method on new settings.
record.gate_note: Rows below record the paper's own measurements and interventions. Cited findings from prior IOI and induction-head studies are not recorded as results. Appendix figures described only qualitatively are included only where the paper states the outcome in text.
record.test_reason: This is the original source for all versions (arXiv:2310.04625). Its own measurements, circuit analyses and ablations bear directly on V1–V6, so it tests the claim. Under the rules it gets no verdict labels. T1 is assigned because it defines the method; the record's T2 is not apt for the source itself.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. The authors claim at least 76.9% of L10H7's role on OpenWebText is copy suppression (by KL), supported by OV and QK weights evidence. They also claim it improves calibration, and that copy suppression explains 39% of self-repair in IOI, with Backup Heads using a different mechanism. They state limits: query inputs are not fully explained, and there is no mechanistic understanding in other models.
record.recipe_differences: This is the source study, not a reproduction of a prior method.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that results depend on the behavioral sample selected (the top 5% by L10H7 effect), on using KL divergence versus loss-based metrics, and on whether an idealized or more faithful input approximation is used. For the query-projection CSPA variant, adding semantic-token subspaces and learned per-token scaling and bias changes recovery from 25% to 61%.
record.problems: The behavioral result is based on a selected top 5% sample rather than an unselected distribution-wide sample. The authors note that their idealized QK setup does not fully represent real functioning, and the 76.9% KL result is not matched by all loss metrics (82% net loss recovery and 45% absolute loss recovery). Transfer to other models is limited and described as weaker or not mechanistically understood. No uncertainty intervals or significance tests are reported in the presented results.
record.rows_left_out: No reported results relevant to the versions were left out. Cited prior-work results and figure values without a textual outcome description were not added as rows.

untested.parts: When and how strongly suppression activates across contexts. The behavioural 80% figure comes only from the top-5% effect sample.
Self-repair via copy suppression outside IOI, and in other models (Appendix Q is only initial).
Mechanistic confirmation in other models and sizes; the authors state they lack it.
The distribution-wide share of self-repair from copy suppression versus LayerNorm or other components. Only IOI is quantified.

missing.what: Query-projection CSPA recovers only 25% of KL naively, and 61% with semantic subspaces plus learned per-token scale and bias.
CSPA-style QK/OV ablations recover more than 50% of KL for many non-negative heads in layers 9–11, which weakens the specificity of the 76.9% figure.
Keyside effective-embedding projection: median attention change -0.09 against mean attention 0.21. The context-free residual gives -0.06.
In 90% of top-10-but-not-top-1 cases, the most suppressed token is semantically related to the source (semantic copy suppression).
L10H7 increases entropy, as do other negative heads.
Patching Name Mover input to Negative Heads from the ABC distribution makes IO-minus-S1 attention 0.08 (L10H7) and 0.0006 (L11H10).
L11H10 backs up L10H7: loss increase is roughly twice as large without controlling the L11H10 path.
A Stanford GPT-2 Small E head self-repairs in IOI but, unlike GPT-2 Small's copy suppression heads, attends equally to IO and S2.
The top-5% sample accounts for half of L10H7's loss-reducing effect. L10H7 is harmful on almost as many completions as it helps.

record.verdict_notes: This is the original source, so no labels are given. Verdicts on versions should come from later studies. Row values match the text.

versions.untested_parts: The paper examines GPT-2 Small, primarily on OpenWebText, rather than establishing the role over every example or all training distributions. It says it does not precisely explain when or how much suppression activates in different contexts.
The 76.9% figure is based on recovered KL divergence, not a claim that the same fraction of every loss effect is explained. The paper also reports distinct loss-recovery measures.
Calibration is assessed with the paper's overconfidence metric on the tested model and distribution; the study does not establish effects on other models or settings.
Self-repair is measured in the narrow IOI task, with the combined contribution of L10H7 and L11H10 reported; the paper does not quantify the effect across the training distribution.

The paper reports limited evidence from IOI, GPT-2 Medium, Pythia, and model classes in an anti-induction comparison. It does not establish that negative heads across other tasks, models, and sizes all implement the same complete role.
The study analyzes self-repair in IOI, not self-repair across the training distribution. It does not quantify the distribution-wide share due to copy suppression versus other mechanisms.

source_check.notes: Appendix D contains a direction inconsistency between its calibration caption and ablation prose. Checks concern this study only; cross-study counts and independent-replication claims cannot be verified from its text.

statements.correction: Section 2.1: 80% within the top-5% loss-effect sample. Sections 3.3.1–3.3.2: CSPA effect averaged over OpenWebText, 76.9% KL recovery; no top-5% completion restriction stated for that aggregate.
statements.problem: The selected behavioural classification is correctly described, but the blanket claim of no measurement on unselected OpenWebText overlooks CSPA.

statements.correction: Section 3.3: 76.9% of L10H7's direct KL effect explained by CSPA over OpenWebText. Section 2.1: 80% behavioural classification within the selected top-5% sample. These are different measures.
statements.problem: It overlooks the original's separate quantitative estimate of overall behaviour explained by CSPA.

statements.correction: Original evidence also includes 76.9% KL effect explained by CSPA averaged over OpenWebText, alongside weights analyses. The three-condition behavioural classification remains restricted to the top-5% sample.
statements.problem: The original's evidence for its principal role does not rest solely on the selected 80% behavioural result.

statements.correction: Appendix B repeats the Section 3.2 QK weights experiment in GPT-2 Medium; the two strongest recovered heads are two of the three most negative IOI heads. Full QK/OV mechanistic confirmation and CSPA recovery in that model are not reported.
statements.problem: The blanket absence of weights-based testing in other sizes overlooks the GPT-2 Medium QK experiment.
The reported direction matches Figure 13b's caption, but Appendix D contains contradictory prose about the direction of the ablation effect.

statements.correction: Appendix D defines an overconfidence metric using the normalized L2 inner product of the model's calibration-curve deviation with the perfectly overconfident reference deviation. Figure 14 illustrates the calibration curves and metric.
statements.problem: Calling the original's overconfidence result merely an unspecified change overlooks its explicit calibration-curve-based metric.
The original's reported decrease follows Figure 13b's caption; its prose about removing L10H7 is internally inconsistent with that direction.

statements.correction: Appendix D explicitly defines and evaluates a calibration-curve-based overconfidence metric under direct-output ablation. Numerical effect sizes and the evaluation dataset are not stated there.
statements.problem: The claim that the original reports no calibration metric is false.

statements.correction: Section 4.1, Equation 4: 39% is the two negative heads' share of total downstream self-repair. It is not reported as 39% of the original Name Mover ablation effect.
statements.problem: It conflates a share of total self-repair with a fraction of the upstream ablation effect compensated.

statements.correction: Appendix B: QK weights experiment repeated in GPT-2 Medium, compared with IOI direct logit attribution. No corresponding GPT-2 Medium OV weights analysis or full mechanistic confirmation is reported.
statements.problem: Describing the GPT-2 Medium evidence as a QK/OV comparison overstates the circuits tested.

statements.correction: Section 4.1: L10H7 and L11H10 jointly explain 39% of downstream self-repair; approximately 61% is the complementary share across other downstream components. Backup Heads exhibit a different mechanism, but no exhaustive allocation of that remainder is stated.
statements.problem: The 39% result is correct, but the entire complementary share is not explicitly assigned exclusively to Backup Heads.

statements.correction: Section 2.1 uses the selected top-5% OpenWebText sample for behavioural classification. Section 4.1 quantifies self-repair on IOI after three Name Mover Heads are ablated; no distribution-wide self-repair share is reported.
statements.problem: The top-5% behavioural sample is not the sample used to quantify self-repair.

statements.correction: Top-5% selection: Section 2.1 behavioural classification. KL versus loss: CSPA recovery. Input approximations: circuit faithfulness. The 39% self-repair share is measured separately on IOI.
statements.problem: These choices concern behavioural classification and mechanism faithfulness; the study does not measure their effect on the self-repair share.

statements.correction: Section 4.2 freezes LayerNorm scaling and projects upstream output changes onto or perpendicular to the IO unembedding. Most Backup Heads retain similar logit differences under perpendicular projection. The 39% allocation comes from the separate Section 4.1 ablation.
statements.problem: The projection interventions establish directional dependence, but no revised allocation of self-repair shares under those interventions is reported.

statements.correction: Main mechanistic analysis: GPT-2 Small. Appendix B: GPT-2 Medium QK test and weaker Pythia instances. Appendix A: GPT/Pythia/SoLU score comparison. Behavioural classification uses the top-5% sample; CSPA's 76.9% KL recovery is averaged over OpenWebText.
statements.problem: The blanket GPT-2 Small restriction contradicts the listed cross-model results, and the claim of no unselected-text behavioural evidence overlooks CSPA.
